analysis.pattern_summary: Across four G3 writing tests (67–80%), Alexandra repeatedly loses points on sentence-level tasks that require following a specific instruction: using a named structure (the "since" conjunction, an appositive), preserving meaning when rewriting (the question rewrite, the stronger-verb rewrite, the fragment fix), and avoiding run-ons (comma splices on G3.3 Q4 and G3.5 Q4). Her one-sentence opinion and response items (G3.2 Q8, G3.3 Q8–9, G3.4 Q7–9) are often short, lack a developed "because" explanation, and contain subject-verb agreement and spelling errors. She also answers conventions-recognition items incorrectly (labeling a declarative sentence "imperative"). Her paragraph responses score comparatively well (70–85%), so the persistent gap is precision at the sentence level.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, subordinating conjunctions (since/because), run-on and comma splice correction, meaning-preserving sentence rewrites, strong or precise verb choice, fragment-to-sentence revision, sentence type identification, subject-verb agreement, explaining reasons and character traits in one sentence, proofreading and spelling, comprehension of the task instruction
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Alexandra shows mastery of Basic Conjunctions, Change Sentence To Question, Fragment Or Sentence, and nearly all Paragraph skills, yet she still fails the matching test items (combining sentences, question rewrites, fragment repair). Short constructed responses often lack a stated reason (G3.1 Q10, G3.5 Q9). Informal, conversational language ("Well…", "want to know?") and spelling or mechanics errors show up throughout. Blank responses on the last three long-form items (G3.5 Q11, G3.6 Q11) and on a sentence-type identification item (G3.2 Q4) suggest disengagement or giving up on the hardest tasks.

analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably hurt G3.2 (a blank on the sentence-type item and thin answers) and G3.5 (a blank final paragraph and run-on sentences), but the same errors appear on non-rushed tests (G3.1 and G3.4), so rushing made things worse without being the root cause.

analysis.pattern_summary: Asher scores 79-89% on every test, yet he stays in the loop because of recurring errors on sentence-level tasks. He loses points on sentence combining and revision, such as ignoring the required connector (because/but/so) or dropping part of the original content when combining. He also loses points on appositives that are too generic, on following precise directions, and on mechanics (spelling, subject-verb agreement, apostrophes, capitalization). His content comprehension is mostly sound, but one-sentence responses (Q7 on the Constitution at 33%, Q4/Q5/Q1 at 50%) show he misreads or misapplies the text and gives incomplete or vague answers. Paragraph responses (Q11, 85%) are consistently good but not flawless.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases (specific/descriptive detail), sentence combining with required conjunctions (because/but/so), preserving all information when combining sentences, modifier placement, converting sentence types (declarative to interrogative), following prompt directions precisely, accurate text-based inference and comprehension, spelling and proofreading, subject-verb and verb-form agreement, apostrophes/capitalization, specific supporting detail in one-sentence responses, effort and engagement on short responses (e.g. "dddddddd")
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The AlphaWrite data is not provided, so mastery there can't be confirmed. Test results do show he can write strong multi-sentence paragraphs (Q11 at 85% every time) yet misses the precise sentence-level mechanics and instruction-following that single-sentence items require. This suggests a disconnect between general fluency and careful, rule-specific execution, which proofreading and revision would address.
analysis.rushing_impact: All five tests were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely caused many of the avoidable losses (typos like "Gradma" and "eachother," skipped required connectors, dropped content when combining, and the "dddddddd" non-response), so it probably cost him the few points separating him from a clean pass.

analysis.pattern_summary: Austin's scores swing between 44% and 89% on G3 writing tests, and the same sentence-level skills fail repeatedly. Appositives (G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q3) are missed both times, and sentence combining with conjunctions or "because" is inconsistent (comma splices, dropped subjects, "string" for "strong"). Question transformation also fails on helping verbs and end punctuation ("Where" for "Were", no question mark). Paragraph tasks (Q11) are uneven: 80% on G3.2, 35% on G3.4, 0% on G3.6 and G3.7 (both blank), then 89% on G3.8. The blanks and the thin G3.4 paragraph point to stamina and task-initiation problems and weak use of text evidence, not just skill gaps. Proofreading is also weak, with recurring errors in spelling, capitalization ("layla", "jason"), homophones ("where/were"), and typos ("at6", "swa").
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences with subordinating conjunctions and keeping both subjects, comma splices and run-ons, converting statements to questions (helping verbs and end punctuation), proofreading (spelling, capitalization of names, homophones), adding reasons or elaboration to one-sentence responses, text-evidence integration in paragraphs, paragraph development and completion (stamina and initiation), sentence type identification, answering "why" questions with a complete main clause
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every G3 skill as MASTERED, including Combine Sentences, Basic Conjunctions, and all paragraph skills, yet tests still show errors in sentence combining, appositives, and paragraph production. Mastery appears to hold only in scaffolded, low-stakes practice and does not transfer to independent, timed test conditions. The AlphaWrite scores are also listed as None%, so the mastery flags can't be checked against actual performance. Appositives don't appear in the plan at all, even though they fail on tests.
analysis.rushing_impact: G3.7 was rushed and likely lowered the score substantially, since the blank Q11 paragraph and the missing feedback and brief answers on Q6 and Q10 suggest disengagement. Even so, the 44% is only slightly below the non-rushed G3.6 score of 48%, which also had a blank Q11, so rushing is not the sole cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): appositives were missed on G3.5 Q4 and G3.6 Q3, and no appositive skill appears in the G3 plan.
- Combine Sentences with Subordinating Conjunctions and Fix Comma Splices (Sentences G3): the student wrote "because" with a comma splice, dropped subjects, and ran sentences together.
- Statements to Questions with Helping Verbs and End Punctuation (Sentences G3): repeated Were/Where and missing question mark errors.
- Proofread and Revise Your Own Writing (Writing Brainlift): recurring spelling, name capitalization, and homophone errors that grader feedback flags on nearly every test.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with Text Evidence, Timed (Paragraphs G3): the paragraph went blank twice and was thin on G3.4. Practice starting independently, using the SPO strategy, and quoting the passage under test-like conditions.

analysis.pattern_summary: Axl's scores (58%, 89%, 78%) show he is not stuck on one weak area. His errors recur at the sentence level and in explaining his reasoning. He often writes fragments or incomplete sentences (G3.3 Q7 gives only an event with no "why"), leaves out end punctuation (G3.2 Q3), and makes agreement and plural errors ("that days," "other" for "others," "camel go's"). He also gives surface answers without a reason or text-based explanation (G3.4 Q6 and Q9 say what Layla likes or what the guide said, not what her actions reveal or how nature influenced her). His sentence combining with "since" shows the wrong cause-effect logic ("Layla saw a butterfly, since she took out her camera"). In G3.2 Q11 the paragraph is short and loosely organized, with no clear topic sentence or supporting evidence, though his G3.3 and G3.4 paragraphs scored 90% and 70%.
analysis.skill_gaps: Complete sentence writing (avoiding fragments), end punctuation for questions, subject-verb and plural agreement, explaining "why" with a reason (claim + reason), inferring character traits from actions, using text evidence in short responses, subordinating conjunction logic (cause/effect with "since"), strong verb revision, paragraph organization and transitions, proofreading and revision of his own work
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Axl has mastered the Subordinating Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, and Paragraph skills in AlphaWrite, yet he misapplied "since" on the G3.4 test and gave an underdeveloped paragraph on G3.2. This suggests his skills do not transfer to independent, timed writing: he can complete the structured AlphaWrite tasks but does not apply the skills or proofread when composing his own responses. The AlphaWrite scores also show as "None%," so mastery may reflect completion rather than demonstrated accuracy.
analysis.rushing_impact: The data does not include rushing flags, but the careless errors (missing question mark, "that days," and answers that don't address "why") suggest rushing or lack of proofreading may have had a moderate effect, though the gaps in reasoning are real skill issues as well.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Subordinating Conjunctions Cause and Effect Practice (Sentences G3): corrects the reversed logic with "since" and "because" seen on G3.4 Q2, using his own sentences rather than given ones.
- Write Complete Sentences / Fix Fragments (Sentences G3): targets the fragment answers (G3.3 Q7) and builds the habit of answering in a full sentence.
- Punctuation and Grammar Proofreading: Question Marks, Plurals, Verb Agreement (Sentences G3): addresses the missing question mark, "that days," "other/others," and "go's."
- Claim + Reason Sentences / Explain Your Thinking (Writing Brainlift): builds the "because" reasoning needed for the "explain why" and character-trait questions (G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q6 and Q9).
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with Text Evidence and Revision Checklist (Paragraphs G3): reinforces topic sentence, details, transitions, and closing, and adds a self-check before submitting.

questions.student_answer: In 1980 in Burkina Faso Yacouba filled 8 inch holes with compost. Each hole, called a zaï, was filled with manure, leaves, other waste, and compost. The land where they lived was in between the rainforests and the Sahara Desert. They had not had good heavy rain in 10 years. Because of this and many people and animals using the land, it had turned dry and cracked. Slowly, but surely the land was turning in to a desert. Yacouba told the people that rain would return and when it did, the seeds would grow. Many people did not believe him. But soon enough, the seeds started to grow at the next rain. The holes had caught the water and the compost had given the plants nutrients. Today greenery grows where a desert once was. Now Yacouba visits other villages and other people and teaches them how to bring life back to a desert. And all over West Africa people make zaï holes along with other ways to save water. And it's all because of Yacouba!
questions.feedback: “The holes had caught the water and the compost had given the plants nutrients” clearly explains how Yacouba’s method worked, using strong details from the article. To make your paragraph even easier to follow, start with a sentence that directly states how both his ideas and his character helped, before telling the events in order. For example: “Yacouba’s smart idea for zaï holes and his belief in his plan helped plants grow even when the land was dry.” Your ending nicely shows that his idea helped people across West Africa.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across all three tests, Aya's main recurring error is comma splices and run-ons. She joins two complete thoughts with only a comma (G4.1 Q1, Q6, Q10; G4.2 Q5, Q9, Q10; G4.3 Q9) and overloads single-sentence prompts with too many ideas. She also struggles with precise sentence construction: she leaves fragments incomplete (G4.3 Q5 has no main verb), misplaces modifiers and word order (G4.3 Q2), misreads what the prompt asks (G4.2 Q4 puts the appositive on the flower rather than the festivals; G4.3 Q9 doesn't answer the question), and uses commas incorrectly (G4.1 Q4). Her paragraph writing is relatively strong (80-90%), so the loop comes from sentence-level control and prompt-targeted revision, and her scores have dropped from 86% to 78% to 71%.
analysis.skill_gaps: comma splices/run-on correction, fragment completion (adding a main verb), word order/modifier placement, appositive targeting (describing the correct noun), subordinate clause punctuation (unneeded comma before "if"/"because"), cause-effect ordering when combining sentences, single-sentence concision, answering the specific prompt, proofreading for word accuracy (swished vs. switched), opening paragraphs with a direct thesis that addresses every part of the prompt
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Aya is marked MASTERED on every G4 skill (basic conjunctions, combining sentences, appositives, fragment vs. sentence) with few attempts (1-3 each), yet she still makes these same errors in timed written responses. This suggests the quizzes check recognition or scaffolded practice but not the independent, self-edited production that the tests require. The best/latest scores are also blank (None%), so mastery may have been reached too easily to be reliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: Only G4.2 was flagged as rushed, and it probably had a modest effect: its error types (comma splices, a missed appositive target) match the un-rushed G4.1 and G4.3, and her biggest drop came in the un-rushed G4.3, so the gaps are real rather than caused by speed.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fragment Or Sentence (Sentences G4): Fragments such as "Nearby, a caterpillar who..." show she doesn't reliably spot a missing main verb. Redo the activity with production tasks (expand a fragment) rather than identification only.
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G4): Her comma splices and cause/effect reversals (G4.1 Q1, Q5) call for a re-attempt with a strict standard: no comma-only joins, and correct order of ideas when using because/but/so.
- Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G4): Practice joining two ideas with a coordinating or subordinating conjunction and correct punctuation, so she stops using commas alone in one-sentence responses (G4.1 Q6, Q10; G4.2 Q9, Q10).
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G4): She wrote an appositive about the wrong noun in G4.2 Q4. Focus on choosing the noun the prompt names and punctuating the phrase correctly.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraph From Prompt G4): Practice opening with a topic sentence that answers every part of the prompt (e.g., "ideas and character" in G4.3 Q11), then add a self-edit checklist for run-ons, verbs, and word choice.

analysis.pattern_summary: Boden's one-sentence responses (G3.2 Q3, Q6, Q7, Q9) show the same errors: fragments starting with "Because," run-on or multi-idea sentences (Q9), no reason or support, and unedited mechanics (lowercase "i" and "hershey," misspellings like "breas," "hoew," "charitey"). When asked to revise or combine sentences, he copies the sentence with new errors (G3.3 Q5 "sigh," "baby"; G3.2 Q1 "454,650") or doesn't do the task (G3.4 Q4 gave unrelated text). He also submits non-attempts on the paragraph task ("vv," "sdw" for 0%), so the loop is driven by sentence-level control, proofreading, and effort on extended responses. The G3.4 paragraph (85%) is polished and far above his earlier writing, so it should be verified as his own work.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence fragments vs. complete sentences, sentence combining with because/but/so (task comprehension), sentence revision for concision (avoiding repeated phrases), proofreading and copy accuracy, capitalization of proper nouns and "I", spelling of high-frequency and text words, adding reasons and text evidence to one-sentence answers, single-sentence control (avoiding run-ons), paragraph writing stamina and task initiation
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every Combining G3 and Paragraphs G3 skill as MASTERED, mostly after 1–2 attempts, yet he still fragments sentences, fails to combine sentences on the test, and leaves paragraph prompts blank. This suggests mastery was reached with little practice and doesn't transfer to independent, timed writing. Also, the AlphaWrite scores are all missing (None%), so mastery can't be verified.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing likely had a large effect, since all three tests were flagged RUSHED, two paragraph responses were gibberish (0%), and most of his errors (typos, capitalization, copied-wrong words) are careless, not conceptual.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Quiz, redo with accuracy goal (Combining G3): he ignored the because/but/so task on G3.4 Q4 and the G3.3 Q5 sentence-completion item, so he should repeat it with a required score threshold, not just one attempt.
- Sentence Fragments and Complete Sentences practice (Sentences G3 / Writing Brainlift): addresses "Because you get to throw teddy bears on the ice" and run-on answers like Q9.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt, with a short timed, supervised repeat (Paragraphs G3): he left paragraph prompts as "vv"/"sdw", so he needs supervised, no-paste practice building a topic sentence plus two text details.
- Elaborate Paragraphs / Elaborate with Reasons (Paragraphs G3): adds "because" reasons and examples, which graders requested on Q5 and Q7.
- Writing Brainlift proofreading/revision checklist routine (capitalization, proper nouns, "I," spelling check before submit): addresses the careless errors and the rushing, and could include a minimum time-on-task before submission.

questions.student_answer: A boy named Jason built two very well done statues in the Caribbean sea. In fact, the first 65 statues were very close to Grenada. questions.feedback: You did a great job sharing facts about Jason and his underwater statues. For example, you could begin: "Jason put his sculptures under the sea to protect coral reefs and sea animals. analysis.pattern_summary: Brenna's weak points are in sentence-level tasks: combining sentences with the required structure (conjunctions "because" and "since", an appositive, "and"), and following the exact task direction (G3.4 Q3 asked for an interrogative and she wrote a statement; G3.4 Q2 asked for "since" and she used "so"; G3.7 Q4 asked for an appositive and she wrote a plain sentence). Her errors also recur in verb tense and subject-verb agreement ("turn/looked," "help/helped," "has help"), run-ons and comma splices, and spelling. Her paragraph responses are decent (55-85%) but lose points to weak development and unclear reasoning, as in G3.7 Q6, where she gave the wrong cause for warm soil, and Q11, where she gave generalities instead of text facts. Her short constructed responses are consistently capped at 50-67%.
analysis.skill_gaps: Sentence combining with specified conjunctions (because/since/and), appositive phrases and comma punctuation, converting sentence types (statement to question), verb tense and subject-verb agreement, run-on and comma-splice correction, concision (removing repeated or added ideas), explaining the "why" with a causal reason, using text evidence in paragraphs, proofreading and spelling, following prompt directions precisely
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: She has mastered the G3 AlphaWrite activities on fragments vs. sentences, topic sentences, transition words, and paragraph writing, yet she still loses points on tests for sentence combining, sentence types, grammar and conventions, and causal explanation. The AlphaWrite plan has no activities at the sentence-manipulation level (combining, appositives, revising) or on proofreading, so her mastery of structure does not carry over to precise, conventional sentence construction.
analysis.rushing_impact: Only G3.2 was flagged as rushed, and the careless errors there (a stray comma after "because," unnecessary capitalization, a repeated phrase, a typo) suggest rushing contributed somewhat, but the same error types appear in her non-rushed tests, so rushing was not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G3): she misplaces commas and uses the wrong connector with "because," "since," and "so," so she needs practice matching the required conjunction.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): she missed the appositive on G3.5 Q4 and G3.7 Q4 (comma use and "that" vs. appositive form).
- Sentence Types: Statements, Questions, Commands (Sentences G3): she answered an interrogative prompt with a statement on G3.4 Q3.
- Fix Run-ons and Verb Tense/Agreement (Sentences G3): she repeatedly makes tense, agreement, and run-on errors in single-sentence responses.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with Text Evidence and Revision/Proofreading (Paragraphs G3): her paragraphs need specific facts from the passage, clear reasons, and a spelling and conventions check before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooke has scored 80-87% on four G3 tests, but she keeps losing points on the same short constructed-response items: the 50% questions that require a specific sentence-combining or revision move (appositive, "since," a concise rewrite) and the 67% one-sentence explanations. She often writes a reasonable, on-topic sentence but skips the structural requirement in the prompt. Examples are "so" instead of "since," no appositive in G3.3 Q3, the wrong placement of the appositive in G3.1, and no action or reason given when the prompt asked for one. Her paragraphs show good ideas and organization, but they are consistently weakened by conventions errors: spelling (famliy, thier, kindess, wrighting), capitalization, run-ons and comma splices, and homophone confusion (there/their, then/than).
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and punctuation, subordinating conjunction use (since), following the prompt's specific task requirement, concise sentence revision (avoiding redundancy and run-ons), elaborating with a reason or action in one-sentence responses, spelling and proofreading, capitalization and sentence boundaries in paragraphs, comma usage, homophones, completing a task fully (G3.3 Q5, which was scored 0%)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Every AlphaWrite G3 skill is marked MASTERED, including appositives, subordinating conjunctions, and combining sentences, yet she still misses these exact skills on tests. The disconnect is that she can do them in scaffolded, isolated practice but doesn't transfer them to open-ended written responses, where she must read the directions closely and proofread. The AlphaWrite data also shows no scores (best/latest = None), so mastery may reflect completion rather than demonstrated accuracy.
analysis.rushing_impact: G3.4 was flagged as rushed, and the short, underdeveloped answers there ("She loves the outdoors," a missing "since") probably cost her a few points. However, she scored 84%, in line with her other attempts, and the same error types appear in the non-rushed tests, so rushing was likely a minor factor.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3, Production G3): she missed appositive tasks on G3.1 and G3.3, so she should redo them with a requirement to check the placement and commas of the appositive.
- Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G3): she substituted "so" for "since" on G3.4, so she needs practice matching the conjunction named in the prompt and building "Since X, Y" sentences.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): her paragraphs have strong ideas but weak conventions, so she should draft and then do a required proofreading pass for capitalization, spelling, and sentence boundaries.
- Writing Brainlift: Respond-to-the-Prompt Checklist: have her underline each requirement in the prompt (action, reason, conjunction, appositive) and confirm each is in her sentence before submitting. This targets the missing action, reason, and structure in one-sentence answers.
- Combine Sentences Quiz (Combining G3): she has a G3.2 run-on and a redundancy error ("that day" twice), so she needs practice on concise, clear, single-sentence revisions.

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooklyn's written-response errors cluster in four areas. Sentence combining with appositives (G3.5 Q4 used "because", G3.7 Q4 added a non-appositive clause). Text-grounded answers (G3.6 Q8 said a porcupine shoots quills, which contradicts the passage; G3.4 Q6 gave a detail but no character inference). Complete-sentence responses that restate the question stem (G3.5 Q6 and Q7). Paragraph writing, which is the most unstable area: scores swung from 90% to 55% to 0%, with two blank submissions on G3.5 and G3.6 and a formulaic "Have you ever wondered…" opening and "In conclusion" ending that leave the middle thin or off-text. Mechanics and conventions (run-on comma splices, "eachother," "conlcusion," vague phrasing like "learn your body") also keep costing points.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, combining sentences without conjunctions, complete-sentence responses that restate the question, text evidence integration and accuracy, character inference/analysis, paragraph development beyond formulaic frames, run-on and comma-splice control, proofreading/spelling, task completion on long written responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Brooklyn has mastered appositive combining and writing, basic conjunctions, and paragraph-from-prompt (5 attempts) in AlphaWrite, yet still defaults to "because" or a relative clause on test appositive items and shows inconsistent paragraph quality. The disconnect is that skills are demonstrated in isolated, scaffolded quizzes but do not transfer to passage-based, unscaffolded prompts where the student must also read accurately and self-monitor. Mastery was reached with few attempts (most 1–2), so it may be shallow.
analysis.rushing_impact: All five tests were flagged as rushed, and the two blank paragraph responses, the unproofread spelling errors, and the passage-contradicting answers suggest rushing substantially depressed outcomes, likely more than a true skill deficit would explain.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives, retake with a mixed review (Production G3): the student still confuses appositives with "because" clauses on tests despite a single-attempt mastery, so more practice is needed.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): reinforce renaming noun phrases set off by commas, particularly "X, famous for…, did Y" structures.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): strengthen the body of the paragraph with accurate, passage-based details in place of generic filler.
- Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraph From Prompt G3): practice with timed, passage-based prompts, including a checklist for finishing and proofreading before submitting, to curb blank or rushed responses.
- Writing Brainlift: Restating the Question in Complete Sentences / Citing Text Evidence: teach turning the question stem into the start of the answer and checking each claim against the passage (for example, the porcupine item).

skills.skill: Transformation G3 Change Sentence Type Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooks can write grammatical, punctuated sentences, but he does not develop or support ideas, so he stays stuck on the extended-response items. He gives fragments or bare answers ("Because it's more fun," "Yes I do," "The sport of hockey") and does not restate the question or give a reason. He also misreads transformation tasks: he added a reason clause instead of making an interrogative, and used "was looking" instead of a stronger verb. In the G3.4 paragraph he organized events in time order but had run-on sentences and spelling errors, and the earlier G3.2 attempt was left blank. The test data also lists his G3.2 score as 29% and G3.4 as 78%, a large jump that suggests inconsistent effort or engagement rather than a steady skill gap.
analysis.skill_gaps: Writing complete sentences that restate the question, supporting answers with reasons, changing sentence type (declarative to interrogative) while keeping the original content, strong or precise verb choice, explaining text evidence (character traits supported by story details), run-on correction and sentence boundaries, spelling of high-frequency and text-based words (Hershey, geode, records, which), staying on task for the prompt (Q7 off-topic), and sustained paragraph writing under test conditions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Brooks is marked MASTERED on Change Sentence Type, Write Paragraph From Prompt, and Write Freeform Paragraph, yet he still turned a statement into a reason clause and wrote run-on paragraphs on the tests. This suggests the AlphaWrite mastery came from a single attempt (1 attempt each, no scores recorded) and has not transferred to independent, unscaffolded test writing. The mastery data is also thin enough that it may overstate his actual skill.
analysis.rushing_impact: There is no explicit rushing data, but the blank Q11 and the very short one-line answers on G3.2 suggest low effort or disengagement that likely depressed that score substantially, while the improved G3.4 result suggests rushing or effort was a larger factor than skill alone.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Change Sentence Type Practice, repeated attempts (Transformation G3): he mastered it on one attempt but still turned a statement into a reason clause instead of a question, so he needs more reps with feedback on keeping the original content.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with revision (Paragraphs G3): focus on topic sentences, supporting reasons, and ending punctuation to reduce run-ons and fix the unfinished or blank paragraph responses.
- Answer in a Complete Sentence / Restate the Question (Sentences G3): targets fragments like "Because it's more fun" and "Yes I do" by teaching him to turn the question into the start of his answer and add "because."
- Strong Verb Substitution (Sentences G3): he replaced "looked" with "was looking," so he needs practice choosing precise, vivid verbs.
- Write Ts From Details with text evidence (Paragraphs G3): builds explaining character traits and why a rule matters using details from the text, as in the Layla and "From Sports and Society" items.

analysis.pattern_summary: Carson's writing is mostly on-topic and ideas are present, but he loses points on sentence-level control in short-response questions. Across all three tests he misses questions that ask him to follow a specific sentence task, such as combining with a required conjunction (G3.2 Q10 "therefor," G3.4 Q2 comma misplacement), rewriting as an interrogative (G3.4 Q3, 0%), or explaining *why* (G3.2 Q7/Q9, G3.4 Q6/Q8 all lack a reason). His paragraph responses (Q11) score 75-80% but lose points to unedited errors: capitalization of names, spelling and homophones (there/their, threw/thrown, stautes, keyna), run-ons, and redundancy ("that day… that day"). The same mechanical errors recur, so he is not catching them by proofreading.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence combining with specified conjunctions (because/but/so/since), comma use after introductory subordinate clauses, sentence types (interrogative transformation), concision and removing redundancy, adding reasons or explanations to short answers, capitalization of proper nouns and sentence starts, spelling and homophones (there/their, threw/thrown, an/a), run-on and fragment correction, proofreading and revising, reading and following task directions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Carson shows Combine Sentences, Subordinating Conjunctions, and all the G3 paragraph activities as mastered after a single attempt each, yet he still misses these exact skills on tests (the "since" and because/but/so combining items, paragraph mechanics). The mastery data has no recorded scores, so it may reflect completion rather than real proficiency, and the skills are not transferring to independent, timed written responses.
analysis.rushing_impact: The rushed G3.4 test (71%) was probably moderately affected: misreading the "interrogative" task and the careless spelling errors ("brezze," "bids," "awsome") look like rushing, but similar mechanical errors on the non-rushed G3.2 test suggest rushing was not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences with Because/But/So (Sentences G3): he ignored the required conjunction on G3.2 Q10 and needs repeated practice with a mastery score threshold rather than one attempt.
- Subordinating Conjunctions: Comma Placement (Sentences G3): he misplaced the comma in the "Since…" sentence (G3.4 Q2), so he needs practice with the comma after an introductory clause.
- Sentence Types: Statements to Questions (Sentences G3): he scored 0% on the interrogative rewrite, which shows he doesn't reliably transform sentence types.
- Add a Reason / Explain Your Answer in One Sentence (Paragraphs G3 or Writing Brainlift): his answers on G3.2 Q7/Q9 and G3.4 Q6/Q8 state an opinion or moment without a "because" reason.
- Proofread and Revise Your Paragraph, with a capitalization/spelling/run-on checklist (Writing Brainlift, Paragraphs G3): his Q11 paragraphs lose points to uncorrected proper nouns, homophones, and run-ons, so he needs a required revision pass before submitting.

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Carter's tests show two different problems. The first is skill: he repeatedly fails appositive construction (G3.5 Q4 and G3.6 Q3 both used "so"/"and" conjunctions instead), he makes basic mechanical errors (capitalization, spelling, unclear phrasing, fragments or question-form answers), and his sentences give no reason or explanation. The second, and increasingly dominant, problem is engagement: scores fall from 49% to 22% as responses turn into refusals or off-topic text ("idk, sorry," "nooppeeeeeeee," "nahhhh," "......really bruh....") on the explanatory sentence and paragraph items (Q6–Q11). Because he does not attempt the paragraph tasks, he never shows whether he can use text evidence or organize a paragraph, and he stays stuck in the loop.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, following the specific task directive (appositive vs. conjunction), complete-sentence writing (fragments, "cuz"/all-caps phrase answers, question-form answers), giving a reason or explanation with "because," text evidence integration, paragraph development from a passage prompt, basic mechanics (capitalization, spelling), sustained effort and persistence on extended-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Carter has mastered nearly every G3 AlphaWrite skill, including both appositive quizzes, Combine Sentences, Fragment or Sentence, and the paragraph-writing skills, yet he still writes conjunction-based combinations when tests ask for appositives and gives non-answers on paragraph prompts. This points to a transfer and motivation gap (the mastery data show no best or latest percentages, so mastery may reflect completion rather than real proficiency) rather than a lack of exposure.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.8 test was flagged as rushed, and his dismissive answers there (0% on three items) fit rushing, but his similar disengaged responses on the unrushed G3.6 and G3.7 tests suggest rushing only added to an existing effort problem.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives, retake with score review (Production G3): he mastered it, but tests show he still swaps in conjunctions, so he needs to redo it with accuracy checks on the appositive form.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): practice placing a comma-set phrase right after the noun, since this was his most consistent test error.
- Paragraph From Prompt: Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraph From Prompt G3): this builds the passage-based paragraph response he skipped on Q11 on all four tests, and should be done with a short, scaffolded passage.
- Elaborate Paragraphs and Write Cs From Details (Paragraphs G3): these target adding reasons and text details with "because" so his one-sentence explanations include evidence.
- Writing Brainlift goal-setting and effort check-in: a short conference using his test responses to address refusals and the drop in effort before the next test, plus a pre-test routine with a required minimum attempt on each item.

It also teaches students to never give up, and to trouble shoot which makes the students become more independent.

He chose "Imperative" for a declarative sentence on both G7.1 and G7.2 (Q2). He picked a plain "and" combination instead of a logical one on G7.3 Q3. He missed topic-fit and "does not belong" questions on G7.2 Q7/Q9, G7.3 Q7 and G7.5 Q10. Spelling errors in the essays ("nescessity," "enviornment," "benifit," "taht") add minor convention losses.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence type identification (declarative vs. imperative), logical sentence combining (cause/contrast relationships), identifying relevant vs. irrelevant sentences, matching supporting sentences to a topic, evidence elaboration and explanation of significance, thesis and body-paragraph variety (avoiding restated sentences), spelling and proofreading
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Cruz shows mastery of Identify Sentence Type, Combine Sentences, Basic and Subordinating Conjunctions, and the Essays G7 Draft, Outline and Polish steps. He still misses the same sentence-type and combining items on tests, and his essays stay at 70%, so the mastery is not transferring to test conditions. The one non-mastered activity, Essays G7 > Identify (5 attempts), matches his test misses on topic relevance and "does not belong" questions. Because AlphaWrite scores show as None, I cannot tell whether "mastered" reflects real accuracy or just completion.
analysis.rushing_impact: The data includes no timing or rushing flags, so I cannot say rushing affected outcomes. The repeated identical wrong answer on Q2 and the spelling slips suggest some inattention, but the consistent 70% essay ceiling points mainly to skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Essays G7 > Identify (Essays G7): this is the only non-mastered activity and targets recognizing which sentences fit or do not fit a topic, which Cruz missed on G7.2 Q7/Q9, G7.3 Q7 and G7.5 Q10. Require accuracy mastery, not just attempts.
- Identify Sentence Type, re-do with a focus on declarative vs. imperative vs. interrogative vs. exclamatory (AlphaWrite Sentences): Cruz chose "Imperative" for declarative sentences twice despite showing mastery. Have him explain why each answer is right or wrong.
- Combine Sentences / Subordinating Conjunctions, with cause-and-effect and contrast items (AlphaWrite Sentences G7): this addresses the G7.3 Q3 miss, where he chose a plain "and" over a logical connection. Add a step where he justifies the relationship between the ideas.
- Essays G7 > Draft, with an elaboration focus (Essays G7): practice adding a "why this matters" sentence after each piece of evidence, to move him past the 70% ceiling set by the grader feedback on G7.2 and G7.4.
- Writing Brainlift evidence-explanation or paragraph-development activity (Writing Brainlift): practice with evidence → explanation → significance, and varying sentence openings so the thesis and body don't restate each other. Pair it with a short proofreading checklist for his recurring misspellings.
analysis.priority: medium. Cruz's scores are in the 70s to low 80s and rising (83% on the latest test), so he is close to passing. The same gaps keep recurring across five attempts, though, so targeted intervention should start soon.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across five G3 tests (29% → 78%), the student repeatedly fails to write complete, elaborated responses. Short-answer items often get fragments or single words ("Restaurants.", "Pet it.", "yes"), with no reason or explanation. Sentence-combining items (appositives, conjunctions) show persistent errors: unneeded commas ("and, colorfull"), "because," used in place of an appositive, and missing words. Paragraph items (Q11) were blank or filler ("mm", "nhh") on G3.2, G3.4 and G3.5. The student also has frequent errors in spelling, capitalization, and verb forms ("gaven", "where climbing", "Excdied", "sipnes"). The G3.6 jump to 78% came with a real paragraph, which suggests the skills are developing but inconsistent. Effort and stamina are also factors.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and punctuation, combining sentences with conjunctions (comma misuse), elaborating with a reason or explanation ("because" clauses), fixing sentence fragments, answering the exact task (e.g., turning a statement into a question), paragraph writing under test conditions (topic sentence plus details), spelling and proofreading, capitalization and verb forms/subject-verb agreement, precise text-based wording (quills vs. tail), persistence on long-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The student shows "MASTERED" on nearly every G3 skill (appositives, conjunctions, combining sentences, paragraph writing) yet repeatedly misses the same skills on tests. Appositive items failed on G3.1 and G3.5 despite 4 attempts on the appositive quiz. Paragraph prompts were left blank or filled with junk despite mastered paragraph modules. This suggests mastery does not transfer to independent, untimed-to-test conditions, or that the student can pass the activities with scaffolds or low effort. Scores show as None%, so the mastery data is hard to verify.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of five tests (G3.1, G3.4, G3.6) were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely contributed substantially on G3.1 and G3.4, where one-word answers and unfinished or filler responses dominated. G3.6 shows that a rushed test can still score high (78%), so the effect there was likely small.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo with a stricter mastery threshold, since the student still writes "because," or adds commas instead of using appositives (G3.1 Q1, G3.5 Q4).
- Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G3): the student has only 1 attempt, and "and," comma errors and missing words persist (G3.2 Q2, G3.5 Q3).
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): the student gives one-word or bare answers with no reason, and has only 1 attempt.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): the student has submitted blank or filler paragraphs on three tests and needs repeated timed practice with topic sentence plus 2 details.
- Writing Brainlift proofreading/editing practice (Writing Brainlift): targets spelling, capitalization, verb forms, and fragments like "Me and my friends, where climbing…" that the student could catch with a self-check routine.

Transformation G4 Change Sentence Type Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: David repeatedly misses sentence-level construction tasks across all three G4 tests. Appositive items (G4.1 Q3, G4.2 Q4, G4.3 Q3) fail every time: he moves the phrase or repeats information already in the sentence, and in G4.3 he described the wrong noun (lettuce instead of Noah's mom). Sentence combining with conjunctions or sentence-type changes (G4.1 Q5 "because due to", G4.3 Q4 missing word and extra comma, G4.3 Q1 repeated "they") breaks down on syntax, and his single-sentence responses (G4.2 Q7, G4.3 Q8, Q9) are scored at 67% for lacking development, run-ons, or no elaboration. Mechanics errors (capitalization of "I," spelling like "recieved," "swiched," "catipiller," "texas," and the dropped words) recur and keep scores from reaching the pass threshold even when his ideas are sound.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (identifying the target noun and adding new information), appositive punctuation and placement, sentence combining with because/but/so (avoiding redundant conjunctions), sentence syntax and word omission, fragment completion with a fragment starter, run-on and comma-splice control, single-sentence elaboration (reasons and details), capitalization and spelling, proofreading and self-editing, paragraph development with specific text evidence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite lists every skill as MASTERED, including Write Appositives, Combine Sentences, and Change Sentence Type, yet these are exactly the question types he fails on tests. The disconnect is that AlphaWrite quizzes likely check recognition or guided practice (1 attempt on most), while tests require independent, error-free production, so mastery is not transferring.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, but the careless errors (dropped words, repeated "they," "because due to," uncapitalized "I") suggest that rushing or lack of proofreading likely contributed moderately to the lost points.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Sentences G4): redo with a focus on choosing the correct noun and adding new information, since he has failed this on all three tests despite a "mastered" status.
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G4): practice with because/but/so and choose only one conjunction, targeting the "because due to" and "so, they could on them" errors.
- Change Sentence Type (Sentences G4): rewrite exclamatory and other sentence types while keeping all words and meaning, to fix the repeated and omitted words.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Writing): add elaboration (reason, detail, example) in each sentence, so one-sentence answers earn full credit rather than 67%.
- Writing Brainlift proofreading and revision routine: a checklist covering capitalization, spelling, missing words, and re-reading each answer aloud before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Davis repeatedly gives answers that are partly correct but incomplete. He states a claim without a reason or example (Q5 "diehards," Q9 "tradition," G3.5 Q6 and Q7), and he does not answer the actual question, such as whether tossing bears is a good way to help others or what a child might feel. He also struggles with sentence combining. He uses a comma splice instead of a conjunction (G3.5 Q3), uses "because of this" in a way that flips the cause and effect (Q2), uses "yet" when told to use because/but/so (Q10), and repeats the time phrase (Q1). His paragraph responses (Q11 on both tests, scoring 65%) are loosely organized, lack a topic sentence and transitions, and contain many spelling and convention errors ("camals," "thier," "accross," "popluar," "know/there/spikes").
analysis.skill_gaps: Elaborating with "because" reasons or evidence, answering the specific question asked (opinion and inference responses), combining sentences with coordinating/subordinating conjunctions, avoiding comma splices, logical cause-and-effect connections, following prompt directions (specified conjunctions), appositive construction, paragraph organization (topic sentence, transitions, concluding sentence), conciseness (removing redundancy), spelling and proofreading, homophones and word endings (there/their, know/known)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Davis is marked MASTERED on Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, Fragment or Sentence, and Unscramble Sentences, yet he still fails to combine sentences with conjunctions and to write an appositive on the tests (G3.5 Q3 and Q4). His skills appear to hold up in isolated, scaffolded practice (each skill shows only 1 attempt and no scores) but not when he has to write independently from a prompt and stimulus, so the mastery data may be too thin or too easy to trust.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.2 test was flagged as rushed, and rushing probably contributed to the careless spelling and punctuation errors and the thin, unelaborated answers, but the same patterns persist on the non-rushed G3.5 test (76%), so rushing is a secondary factor and the main cause is skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3), repeated with higher difficulty and more attempts: Davis's single-attempt mastery doesn't transfer, so he needs more practice choosing the right conjunction (and/but/so/because) and avoiding comma splices.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how students learn new languages in effective ways.

Use information from the passage to support your ideas.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each point with facts or examples from the passage and explain what they show (5 points)

**Stay organized and on topic**
questions.student_answer: In a busy neighborhood café, people speak many different languages. A family at one table talks in Spanish. At the counter, a worker sings along to a French song on the radio. Scenes like this happen across the United States, a country shaped by immigrants. Even though English is the most common school language, many Americans grow up using two languages at home and in their communities. Learning multiple languages can help people in many different ways. Studies show it can help with memorization and improve resilience and problem-solving skills. Studies also show that infants and younger kids learn faster and have an easier time using proper pronunciation. As a result, many families have started teaching kids second languages while they are infants. One of many ways children can learn is through immersion. Immersion is a class where the teachers use the language during all parts of the day, from simple conversation to learning new subjects. Using the immersion method can help kids hear the language and figure out the vocabulary. One other helpful method uses real communication. Some classrooms connect students with pen pals across the globe. When students reach out to them, they create a bond. This bond can help kids find motivation to learn their language to understand the culture of their pen pal. In conclusion, learning a second language is important for understanding immigrants and peers. Learning a new language can help a child grow their brain and understand others' culture. Languages can be taught in multiple different ways, including immersion and talking to pen pals. Children can also be taught at a young age to make pronunciation easier. Languages have many purposes in a child's brain, but the main reason is to help others share culture and feel welcome.
questions.feedback: You clearly explain several effective ways students can learn languages, including starting young, using immersion, and communicating with pen pals. Your explanation that pen pals can motivate students to practice so they can understand another culture is especially strong. To make your essay easier to follow, separate it into five paragraphs: an introduction with your main claim, one paragraph for each learning method, and a conclusion. This structure will help each important idea stand out and give your reader clear pauses between your points.

questions.student_answer:
For many years, the Mithi River in Mumbai, India, was full of trash. Factories dumped waste into the water. Sewage flowed in every day. The river turned black, and it smelled so bad that people stayed away.

When hope seemed lost, a group called Earth5R showed up. They wanted to return the river to its original beauty. They knew it would take hard work and sacrifice. They also knew they could not do it alone.

First, the group mapped out the river and marked the parts that needed the most cleaning. They took water samples to see where the waste was affecting the river most. Then, they held a volunteer event where anyone could come and help the river flourish. At first, few community members came. But soon, more and more people joined. After a few months, the group had removed over fourteen tonnes of trash.

Over time, the river began to return to its original state. Tests showed the water was twenty percent cleaner than before! Eventually, the community started hanging out near the river again.

The project helped the community grow and flourish. It taught the people that everyone should play their part, and not just let the professionals handle it. Volunteers learned to work together as a community and realize that regular people can take action too. Currently, the community holds cleanups to maintain the river's condition and keep it the same for years.
questions.feedback: You clearly describe how Earth5R brought volunteers together, especially when you explain that more people joined the cleanup and removed “over fourteen tonnes of trash.” Your final paragraph also thoughtfully explains the community’s lesson that regular people can take action instead of waiting for professionals. To make your explanation stronger, add more sentences that show why each example of teamwork mattered, not just what happened. For example, after describing the cleanup, you could write, “Because families, schools, and shops worked together, they could remove far more trash than Earth5R could have removed alone.”

analysis.pattern_summary: The student repeatedly misses the same two kinds of questions. On "because" and conjunction items (Q3 on G6.2, G6.3, G6.4 and G6.6), they choose sentences with a comma before or after "because" ("planted milkweed, because…", "because, the animals…"). They also miss the appositive item (picking a "who works as…" relative clause) and the elaboration item (picking a generic restatement). On the Q11 essays, the failing attempts (45-67%) score low for weak organization (a single block with no topic sentences) and for details that are listed or copied from the passage without being put in the student's own words or explained. The two 87% tests (G6.4, G6.5) show the student can write a hooked, multi-paragraph essay, so the problem is inconsistency, not an inability to write.
analysis.skill_gaps: comma use with subordinating conjunction "because", appositive identification (vs. relative clauses), elaboration vs. restatement, paragraph organization with topic sentences, paraphrasing passage evidence in own words, explaining why evidence matters (analysis), proofreading and basic mechanics (e.g., capitalization), consistency under timed conditions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The student has mastered Combine Sentences, Subordinating Conjunctions, Basic Conjunctions and Essays G6 Revise/Polish, yet still misses "because" punctuation on four tests and writes weak essays. This suggests the skills are not transferring to independent test conditions, and "Essays G6 > Identify" (the only unmastered item) may be where the planning and organization gap sits.
analysis.rushing_impact: All six tests were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely had a large effect, since the repeated Q3 errors are surface-level punctuation slips the student should be able to catch (they already mastered the related AlphaWrite skills) and the essay scores swing between 45% and 90%.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Essays G6 > Identify (Essays G6): the one unmastered essay skill, and it targets the planning and organization weakness (topic sentences, separate paragraphs) cited in the grader feedback.
- Subordinating Conjunctions: Comma Placement with "Because" (Combining G6): the student passed the quiz but still misses this on tests, so a targeted redo focused on "no comma before 'because'" should help the knowledge transfer.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G5): the student chose a relative clause over an appositive on G6.6 Q4, so they need practice telling the two apart.
- Elaboration and Paraphrasing Evidence (Writing Brainlift): the student needs practice turning passage details into their own words and adding a "this matters because…" explanation, which the G6.6 feedback specifically recommends.
- Essays G6 > Revise with a self-check checklist (Essays G6): reinforces proofreading for capitalization, comma use and paragraph breaks before submitting, to counter the effect of rushing.

analysis.pattern_summary: Emiliano can usually get a correct idea down, but he loses points on sentence boundaries and mechanics. He writes run-ons with no end punctuation (Q6, Q9, Q10), leaves names and "i" uncapitalized, and writes fragments where full sentences are required (Q8). On G3.2 he also misses the task type. He wrote a statement when asked for a question (Q3), mislabeled a declarative sentence as imperative (Q4), and restated a passage fact instead of making an inference about the fans (Q5). He seems to overapply the appositive from G3.1, inserting inaccurate ones like "a toy store" and "a nice librbrary." His Q11 "paragraph" is one long, tangled sentence with no organization.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence boundaries and run-on correction, end punctuation and comma use, capitalization of proper nouns and "i", sentence types (declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory), converting statements to questions, writing complete sentences instead of fragments, appositive use (accuracy and purpose), concise sentence revision and modifier placement, giving reasons with "because", answering inference questions about the text, paragraph structure (topic sentence, supporting details, conclusion), spelling and proofreading (homophones such as here/hear, plus commonly misspelled words)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: No AlphaWrite data was included, so I can't identify specific mastered skills. The test data does show he can combine ideas and gives relevant, detailed answers, so his ideas and basic sentence formation seem to be in place. The likely disconnect is that he can do these skills in isolation but doesn't apply them on open-ended prompts, where he doesn't proofread or check what the prompt asks for.
analysis.rushing_impact: No timing data was provided, so the effect can't be measured. Unproofread errors such as lowercase "i" and "here" for "hear," along with answers that ignore the task (Q3, Q5), suggest that rushing or not rereading may account for a moderate share of the lost points.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fix Run-On Sentences and Comma Splices (Sentences G3): his answers on Q6, Q9, Q10, and Q11 chain ideas together without punctuation.
- Capitalization and End Punctuation Review (Grammar/Mechanics G2–G3): he repeatedly misses capital letters on names and "I," which cost him points on nearly every response.
- Identify and Convert Sentence Types (Sentences G3): he mislabeled a declarative sentence as imperative (Q4) and could not rewrite a statement as a question (Q3).
- Appositives: Purpose and Accuracy (Sentences G3): he adds inaccurate or unneeded appositives, so he needs practice using them only when they add true, relevant information.
- Writing Brainlift: Plan and Write a Single Paragraph with Reasons (Paragraph Writing G3): he needs a topic sentence, a "because" reason, and supporting details from the text, and a final proofreading checklist (capitals, periods, spelling, "does this answer the question?") would address the Q5 and Q11 problems.

questions.student_answer: Animated movies are fun and colorful. Many children love watching them. But these movies do more than just entertain. They can also teach important lessons about life, feelings, and how to treat others. In many animated movies, characters face big problems. Sometimes, they lose something they love or make a mistake. They often have to find courage to fix things or try again. When children see this, they learn that it's okay to make mistakes and that trying again is part of growing. Animated movies also show how to be kind and honest. For example, a story might show a character helping a friend or telling the truth even when its hard. These moments can help children understand right and wrong. These films often include teamwork and friendship. Characters learn to listen, forgive, and work together. This helps young viewers understand how to solve problems with others. Another good thing is that many animated movies show different people, places, and ideas. This helps children learn about the world. They can become more open to new thoughts and caring about others who are different from them. While movies can't replace real-life lessons from parents and teachers, they can still help. Watching stories about bravery, kindness, and hope can make children think about how they can in their own lives.
questions.feedback: You included important examples from the passage, such as characters trying again after mistakes, showing kindness, and working as a team. These examples clearly connect animated movies to life lessons for children. Next, put the ideas into your own words and explain why each example matters; for example: “When children watch a character keep trying, they may feel braver about fixing their own mistakes.” Organize these ideas into separate paragraphs so each lesson has its own space. Also check small word choices, such as using “it’s hard” and ending with “how they act in their own lives.”

analysis.pattern_summary: Emma's main barrier is task avoidance and low writing confidence, not a single sentence-level skill. On G6.1 and G6.3 she refused the extended expository essay (Q11) with statements like "I am not good at it" and "I am not writing this no matter what," which gave her little or no credit. On G6.2 she did attempt it and earned a 67%. The grader noted she listed passage examples but did not put them in her own words or explain why they matter. That points to gaps in elaboration and in synthesizing text evidence, and the avoidance appears to come from a fear of failure. The weighting of Q11 also varies (15%, 50%, 10%), so a refused essay can hurt the score a great deal.
analysis.skill_gaps: Writing task initiation and persistence, expository essay development, elaboration and explaining evidence, paraphrasing source text, text evidence integration, writing self-efficacy and growth mindset, constructing a thesis or claim sentence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Emma is marked MASTERED on every Essays G6 stage (Outline, Draft, Revise, Polish) and on sentence combining, transitions, and topic sentence skills, yet she refuses or only partly completes the same kind of task on tests. The disconnect is between performing with scaffolds in AlphaWrite and writing independently under test conditions, and it is driven by confidence and motivation more than by skill. The best/latest scores are also missing (None%), so the mastery flags may not reflect real proficiency.
analysis.rushing_impact: All three tests were flagged RUSHED, and rushing likely made a significant difference, since the refusals and the short, unelaborated responses suggest she was not giving the essay real time or effort.
analysis.recommended_activities:

- Essays G6 Revise, focused on elaboration (Essays G6): she needs practice turning listed passage examples into explained points in her own words ("this matters because...").
- Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details (AlphaWrite Paragraph Skills): repeat it with passage-based tasks so she practices a clear claim and supporting details tied to text evidence.
- Writing Brainlift growth-mindset or low-stakes writing sprint (Writing Brainlift): short, ungraded timed writes (5-10 minutes) with positive feedback, to reduce fear of failure and rebuild confidence in writing.
- Paraphrase and Cite Text Evidence (AlphaWrite): practice restating passage details and adding an explanation sentence, which addresses the grader's main feedback from G6.2.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across all three tests, the student fails the sentence-manipulation items (appositive, combine sentences, rewrite as a question), which are consistently worth 50% and scored at or near 0. In G3.1 and G3.3 they restated or joined the ideas without an appositive or true combination. In G3.4 they rewrote the sentence as a statement instead of a question. The student also loses points on one-sentence response items because they give a claim without a "because" reason, and on mechanics: comma splices, run-ons, fragments ("Layla jogging to the guide"), missing end punctuation, lowercase "i," and spelling. The paragraph items (Q11) show the same problems at a larger scale: weak organization, run-ons, repeated words, and thin development, with scores of 30%, 90%, and 60%.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and punctuation, combining sentences into one grammatical sentence, converting statements to interrogatives (following the directive), supporting claims with reasons ("because" elaboration), complete sentences vs. fragments, run-ons and comma splices, end punctuation and capitalization, spelling and verb tense/usage ("brang," "release"), paragraph organization and text-evidence development
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The student is marked MASTERED on Write Appositives, Combine Sentences With Appositives, Combine Sentences, Change Sentence To Question, and Fragment Or Sentence, yet they still miss exactly these skills on tests. This suggests mastery is not transferring: the AlphaWrite data shows only 1 attempt per activity with no recorded scores, so mastery may reflect shallow practice, and the student does not apply the skills to open-ended written prompts with a stimulus.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, so its effect can't be determined, though the careless errors (missing question marks, "playing playing," "to to," and lowercase "i") suggest unedited, fast writing that may have cost some points.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): Re-do with a high accuracy threshold and multiple attempts, since the student missed the appositive and combining items in G3.1 and G3.3 despite "mastered" status.
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3): Practice placing the appositive right after the noun with correct comma use, using prompts like "My family has two dogs, Lucy and Rocket."
- Change Sentence To Question (Sentences G3): Repeat with varied sentence types, and add a checklist (rewrite as a question, not a description, with a question mark) to fix the G3.4 Q3 miss.
- Write Sentence From Prompt (Sentences G3): Practice one-sentence answers with a "because" reason, plus a self-edit step for capitalization, end punctuation, and spelling.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): Practice organizing a paragraph with a topic sentence, details from the text, and complete sentences, while fixing run-ons and comma splices (Writing Brainlift revision/editing practice if available).

skills.skill: Paragraph From Prompt G4 Write Paragraph From Prompt Quiz
Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Evelyn repeatedly fails to produce appositives. She writes a prepositional phrase in G4.1 ("from Kenya, Africa"), embeds a long clause in G4.2, and uses "so" in G4.5, so she can't build a noun phrase that renames the subject. Her paragraph responses (Q11 on every test) are one or two sentences that make a correct general claim but lack specific text details, elaboration, and organization, which holds scores at 35-75%. She also makes many convention errors (spelling such as "becouse," "exited," "acheve," and "socker"; verb tense and agreement; word order; article use; and a missing or run-on structure in G4.3 Q4) that cost points on tasks where her content is otherwise sound.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (noun phrase renaming a noun, set off by commas), combining sentences with conjunctions while keeping the sentence complete and grammatical, paragraph development (multiple supporting details with text evidence), elaboration beyond a single claim, spelling of common and grade-level words, proofreading and editing, verb tense and agreement in transformed sentences (e.g., question formation), sentence word order and fragment expansion, sustained effort on extended responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Evelyn has mastered Identify Appositives, Production G4 Write Appositives, Combine Sentences, Elaborate Paragraphs, and Change Sentence Type in AlphaWrite, yet she still fails appositive, combining, question-transformation, and paragraph items on the tests. This points to a transfer gap: she succeeds in scaffolded, isolated practice but doesn't apply the skills or proofread in open-ended, text-based writing. The AlphaWrite data also shows only 1-2 attempts per skill and no recorded scores, so "mastered" may reflect shallow evidence.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G4.2 test was rushed, and the blank Q11 (0%) probably pulled the score down substantially (potentially 15-25 points), though the appositive error on Q4 shows rushing was not the sole cause of her struggles.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Production Write Appositives, Revisited with Text Prompts (AlphaWrite, Sentences G4/G5): she can identify appositives but fails to produce them in context, so practice should require rewriting sentences with a renaming noun phrase and checking that it is not a prepositional phrase or "so" clause.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G5): she turns appositive combinations into compound sentences with "so," so she needs contrast practice between conjunction and appositive combining.
- Elaborate Paragraphs with Text Evidence (AlphaWrite / Writing Brainlift): her Q11 responses give one general claim and no specific details, so she needs practice adding 2-3 details from the article, with a claim-evidence-explanation frame.
- Proofreading and Editing Checklist for Spelling and Conventions (Writing Brainlift): she loses credit on words like "because," "excited," "achieve," and "soccer," and on verb tense, so a routine of reviewing each response before submitting would help.
- Change Sentence Type with Verb Tense Practice (AlphaWrite): her question rewrite kept the wrong verb form ("began"), and fragment expansion produced awkward word order, so she needs more drills with correct auxiliary verbs and natural sentence order.

analysis.pattern_summary: Golda's ideas are generally sound and on topic. Her scores sit at 67-80% because her sentences lack punctuation, run together, and have frequent spelling errors. Her one-sentence responses also leave out the "because" reason that graders keep asking for (G3.2 Q5, Q7, Q8, Q9; G3.3 Q9; G3.4 Q7). She often misreads or ignores the task directive, such as rewriting a sentence instead of naming its type (G3.2 Q4), omitting "since" in a combining task (G3.4 Q2), and using "then" instead of a causal conjunction (G3.2 Q2). Her paragraph responses (Q11 each time) get 65-75% because of spelling, run-ons, and unclear links between ideas.
analysis.skill_gaps: Run-on sentences and punctuation between independent clauses, spelling of grade-level and passage words, subordinating conjunction use (since/because) in combining tasks, adding a reason or elaboration to one-sentence responses, reading and following the task directive, capitalization and contractions, proofreading and revision, cause-effect connections in paragraphs, verb tense consistency
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Golda has mastered Subordinating Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Identify Sentence Type, and Basic Conjunctions in AlphaWrite, yet she missed the same skills on tests: "since" (G3.4 Q2), "because" (G3.2 Q2), and sentence type (G3.2 Q4). The gap is in transferring these skills to open-response writing and in following directions, not in knowing the concepts. AlphaWrite also doesn't seem to cover punctuation, spelling, or run-on correction, and its recorded scores are blank (best/latest = None), so it's unclear how strong her mastery really is.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.2 test was rushed and had her lowest score (67%), with several careless errors (misspellings like "there," "throown," and rewriting instead of answering Q4), so rushing probably contributed moderately, but the same punctuation, spelling, and elaboration issues persisted on the non-rushed tests, so it is not the main cause.

- Fix Run-On Sentences (Sentences G3): Her responses often join two complete ideas with no punctuation (e.g., "People love this event it sells out every year").
- Subordinating Conjunctions, with open-response retry (Sentences G3): She mastered the quiz format but still omits "since" and "because" when writing her own sentences, so she needs production practice with a reason included.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with a proofreading/revision step (Paragraphs G3): Q11 paragraphs lose points for spelling, punctuation, and unclear connections, so a self-edit checklist should be added.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer the Question Completely (Because/Reason Sentences): She needs to practice restating the prompt, answering it, and adding "because" plus a reason in one punctuated sentence.
- Writing Brainlift: Read the Directions, Then Respond (Task Verb Check): This addresses mismatched answers like rewriting instead of naming the sentence type, and the rushed work on G3.2.

Based on the passage '*A Day in the Life Aboard the International Space Station*', write an **expository essay** explaining **how astronauts adapt their daily routines to living in microgravity aboard the International Space Station**.

Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**
questions.student_answer:
Astronauts have to switch up their life style to live on the ISS. One example of this is how they have to change their basic hygine in the morning. Astronauts adapt their daily routines to living in microgravity aboard the ISS.

One daily routine that the astronauts have to adapt is their morning routine. The normal morning routine would be almost impossible to do in microgravity becuase water and liquids would just float around in little orbs, and clothes dift around. They way that astronauts adapted to this is by making toothpaste edible, and securing cloths to a rack. In conclusion, the normal morning routine wouldn't work in microgravity so astronauts adapted it to work with secured items and edible toothpaste.

Meals are also much different. Breakfast is quick becuase the crew needs to spend the day with reasearch. Most meals are dehydrated and astronauts add hot water to rehydrate them. Crumbs can float around and get into equipment, so they only eat food that stay together. Eating on the ISS and in microgravity is very difficult for astronauts to do safely and efficiantly; however, the people on the ISS adapted their ways of eating to safely eat in microgravity.

Exercise is very important on the ISS becuase musles with weaken faster in microgravity. The people on the ISS made special tredmeals and other devises for the crew to get exercise. Astronauts work out for two hours each day to make sure that they are in tip top shape when they reture to earth. Exercising in mircogravity is super important, so the people on the ISS made special adaptments.

Astronauts adapted to the microgravity in outerspace. An example of this is how they adapted their mourning routine to work in microgravity. without adapting to microgravity spacetravel and working in space would not be possible. As a famous scientist said, "without adaption equals extiction."
questions.feedback: You clearly explain several important adaptations, including securing clothes, choosing foods that do not make crumbs, and exercising for two hours each day. Your essay also follows a clear order, moving from morning routines to meals and exercise. To strengthen your explanation, go beyond saying that astronauts “adapted” and explain exactly why each change helps them in microgravity. For example, you could write, “Securing clothes to storage racks prevents them from floating away, so astronauts can find what they need and keep the station organized.”

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
The passage *The Road Ahead: How Self-Driving Cars Work* explains how self-driving cars work and discusses their potential benefits and concerns.

Write an expository essay explaining why it is important for readers to understand both the benefits and concerns of self-driving car technology before self-driving cars become more common.

Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Intro
questions.student_answer:
Most people believe that self-driving cars will be the future of transportation. They believe this because they will allow people who cannot drive to have the freedom to travel. However, it is important for people to understant both the benefits and the concerns of self-driving cars before they become more common.

First, let's talk about the benefits of new self-driving cars. One benefit is that self-driving cars should stay focused and stop crashes caused by human error. The self-driving aspect of it would allow people who might not be able to drive, like elderly or disabled people, to have the freedom to travel again. Self-driving cars give many benefits to the community.

On the otherhand, many people have concerns about self-driving cars. One concern is what happens if a car fails? In one driving test conducted in Arizona, the car sensed the person but fail to stop in time. One other concern is that many people will lose their jobs. Right now in the USA, millions of people work driving cars and trucks. In summary, tons of people have concerns about self-driving cars, such as that many people will lose their jobs.

There are also some legal questions about self-driving cars. Such as, what happens when a self-driving car gets into a crash? Who would be to blame? The owner? The manufacturer? The software company? Who would the other rider sue? These questions also need to be answered before self-driving cars become more common.

It's important for people to understand the benefits and concerns before making a desision, or explaining the conflict to other people. Self-driving cars, like all new inventions, should always be questioned before becomming common. The benefits and concerns for making any new product or invention are always important for people to understand, so that they can grasp what they are voting for.
